title: Saragarhi, 1897
hookLine: twenty-one Sikh soldiers hold a signal post against thousands on the frontier
last: SINGH SABHA — RENEWAL BEGINS AT SCHOOL.

lines: A SIGNAL POST BETWEEN TWO FORTS.
cards: Some jobs look small until the moment they aren't. The lifeguard watching an empty pool all summer. The night nurse checking the same monitors.
The person keeping a signal lamp lit on a hill so two forts can talk to each other. Nobody writes songs about the quiet days.
But on a September morning in 1897, on a ridge on the northwest frontier, the quiet job became the whole world for twenty-one men.

teach.h: A SIGNAL POST ON THE SAMANA RIDGE.
teach.b: Saragarhi was a little stone post on the Samana ridge, in the mountains of what is now northwest Pakistan.
Its job: pass signals by heliograph, flashes of sunlight from a mirror, between two larger British forts that couldn't see each other.

Twenty-one soldiers of the 36th Sikhs, a Sikh regiment of the British Indian Army, held it under Havildar Ishar Singh. The region was in revolt; local Pashtun tribes were fighting to keep the British out of their valleys.
On the twelfth of September, several thousand tribal fighters surrounded the post. Popular retellings say the defenders were offered safe passage if they gave it up.
They stayed, and held for hours against far greater numbers.
The signaler, Gurmukh Singh, kept flashing messages to the fort, reporting the fight as it happened, until the very end.
Then, the story goes, he asked permission to leave his post, picked up his rifle, and fought until he fell.
All twenty-one died. Each was given the highest gallantry award then open to Indian soldiers.
Sikhs, and the Sikh Regiment of the Indian Army today, remember the twelfth of September as Saragarhi Day, and often tell it alongside the old Khalsa stories of saint-soldiers who stood their ground.
Remember too that the men on the other side were fighting for their own homes. The lesson Sikhs draw isn't about them. It's about twenty-one people who stayed at a small post when staying mattered.

how: Sikhs and the Sikh Regiment of the Indian Army mark Saragarhi Day each year on 12 September; memorial gurdwaras for the twenty-one stand in Amritsar and Ferozepur.

games.q: you're one of twenty-one at a small signal post. thousands are coming. you're offered safe passage if you give up the post. what do you do?
games.why: the twenty-one stayed and held for hours. all of them died at their post.

practice: Think of one small duty that others quietly depend on: picking up a child, answering the email that keeps a project moving, showing up on time for a shift. Picture the people who'd feel it if you let it slide.
Then see yourself holding that post fully, without cutting corners, whether or not anyone notices.
